text:
Moth and Gravel. Field Note 18.
The card says what the TV said.

An AI narrated edition of the
published note. Sofa Remote is a

phone remote for one kind of
television. At the top of its

screen sits a card. On or off,
the channel, the program and its

times, the volume. It looks like
a window onto the TV. It is not

One. The phone cannot see the
TV. Everything on the card is

something the TV said when it
was last asked. That would

hardly matter if the phone were
the only remote in the room. It

never is. The TV has its own
remote. A games console can take

the screen back over HDMI. A
sound bar can move the volume.

Any of them can make the card
wrong without telling the phone.

A claim with an age. The first
version asked about power only

when it believed the TV was off.
On the second day, testing on a

tablet, we switched the TV off
with its own remote. The app

kept showing it on. The fix was
to keep asking. While the remote

is on screen, it asks the TV's
power every 5 seconds in every

state and reconnects when the
answer differs from the card.

Switching the TV on and off with
its own remote then showed up in

the app within about 4 seconds.
The program line has the same

problem in a quieter form.
Broadcast data often switches

late, so the TV can report a
program after it has ended. The

card asks again just after the
program should end, and if the

old one is still reported, every
20 seconds for up to 15 minutes.

None of this makes the card
current. It keeps the card's age

short and its errors temporary.
5 seconds is a choice between a

phone that asks too often and a
picture that stays wrong for too

long. Can't reach is a
conclusion.

Silence from the TV is harder to
read. The first request after

the app opens can fail simply
because the phone's Wi-Fi is

still waking up. So before the
app says it cannot reach the TV,

it asks once more, 2 seconds
later. When it does say so, it

names only a cause it can see
from the phone. These are its

words with the TV's name where
we write the TV. With can't

reach the TV, this device isn't
connected to a network. Can't

reach the TV, this device is on
mobile data. Connect it to your

home Wi-Fi. Can't reach the TV,
a VPN is on. Turn it off or

allow local network access in
the VPN app. Can't reach the TV,

check that it's plugged in and
on the same network as this

device. The app does not guess
that the TV is broken or

unplugged at the wall. It cannot
see either. When no cause on the

phone explains the silence, the
last message says what to check,

not what happened. Reads retry,
keypresses never do. Asking

twice is safe, pressing twice is
not. The project's own rules put

it plainly. Never retry a failed
keypress automatically. A read

that fails can be asked again. A
key that may already have

reached the TV cannot be sent
again without the risk of doing

it twice. Power is where that
bites. The TV takes seconds to

switch, so a second tap on power
soon after the first is almost

always a double tap or an
impatient retry. Sending it

would switch the TV straight
back. The remote lets one power

toggle through every 4 seconds
and ignores the rest.

Ad break follows the same rule
from the other side. One tap

mutes the TV for 3 minutes and
brings the sound back by itself.

It never toggles. It unmutes
only a mute it made and still

holds. A mute by hand, an unmute
with the TV's own remote, or a

phone call that takes the mute
over is left alone.

2 days, 1 TV. The first commit
was on the 25th of October. Most

of what this note describes was
fixed on the 26th on real

hardware after the code had
already passed its tests against

simulated TVs. Each of these
faults appeared only with a real

TV in the room. The power state
went stale after the TV's own

remote was used. Without exact
alarms, Android ended an ad

break about 2 minutes late, so
the app now says so when a break

starts. Every install made its
fast key certificate with the

same subject and serial number,
so pairing a tablet quietly

unpaired the phone. A scene
switched channel and a games

console took the screen back a
moment later. Scenes now look

again 4 seconds later and switch
once more. The tests were

useful. They could not have
found these.

Study scope, 1 TV, 2 days. What
this remote has been tried on.

Sofa Remote is our own Android
app in preparation for Google

Play. It has not been released.
It was built and tried over 2

days with 1 TV, a 2018 Sony
Bravia running Android TV, plus

a phone and a tablet. Other
Bravia models with IP control

should work, but are unverified.
The timings come from the

project commit history and its
own testing on that TV, not from

a measured study. Sony, Bravia,
Android TV, and PlayStation are

named only as the hardware it
works with. The app is not

affiliated with them. You have
been listening to Moth and

Gravel Field Notes. The written
edition is at mothandgravel.com.
